newsitem.title: USA: U.S. unplanned pregnancy rate high - researcher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. unplanned pregnancy rate high - researcher.

text.p: Even though 98 percent of American women use some form of contraception during their reproductive years, about two-thirds still have an unplanned pregnancy, a researcher said on Monday.

More than half of all pregnancies are unintended and about one-quarter of all pregnancies end in abortion, according to Jacqueline Forrest, vice president for research at The Alan Guttmacher Institute in New York.
U.S. levels of unplanned pregnancy and abortion are higher than in many other countries, including Canada, England, Sweden and the Netherlands.

"Helping couples be better contraceptive users can substantially lower levels of unplanned pregnancy and abortion in the U.S.," Forrest said at the American Medical Association's science reporters conference.
"Contraceptive effectiveness would improve if ongoing support is provided rather than assuming that once given a prescription or method, that's the end of the provider's responsibility," she added.
The Alan Guttmacher Institute, a non-profit corporation for reproductive health research, attributed the high levels of unplanned pregnancy to non-use of contraception and contraceptive failure.

Ten percent of women report using no contraceptive, usually because of gaps between stopping one method and starting another. Non-use of contraception accounts for 1.9 million or 53 percent of all unplanned pregnancies and up to 49 percent of all abortions each year, the conference heard.

During the first year of use, an average of eight percent of those using oral contraceptives and 15 percent of those using condoms become accidentally pregnant, primarily because of misuse, Forrest said.

To lower levels of unplanned pregnancies, she said, women and men need easier and affordable access to contraceptive service providers. To improve effectiveness, they need a choice of methods to choose one that suits their needs, she said.

Forrest said many people, especially those with low incomes, are barred from contraceptive choice by financial barriers. "There is a problem as far as financial access, not only to low-income women on Medicaid, but even people who have private insurance, which often doesn't cover contraception care," she said.
